source: Myakala, Agrawal, Manche (2026) BeliefShift: Benchmarking Temporal Belief Consistency and Opinion Drift in LLM Agents
finding: Multi-session benchmark of belief updating. Models that track real updates well resist drift poorly, and the reverse. RAG over past sessions improves update tracking but not drift resistance.
numbers: 2,400 trajectories (960 human-written, 1,440 synthetic); 7 models, zero-shot and RAG. Metrics BRA/DCS/CRR/ESI, e.g. one row 0.83/0.61/0.81/+0.42 (layout garbled in text; model-to-row mapping uncertain). RAG: mean +0.09 BRA, +0.07 CRR, +0.02 DCS. Claude 3.5 Sonnet highest DCS (0.79 zero-shot, 0.81 RAG). GPT-4o RAG BRA 0.83 with DCS 0.61. Krippendorff alpha 0.81 (belief state), 0.76 (contradiction resolution).
quote: No model achieves high scores on both BRA and DCS simultaneously.
limits: Independent-researcher preprint, 60% synthetic trajectories, belief means a user stance not a mapping, no peer review. Table text garbled.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a stability-versus-adaptability trade-off: a mapping store needs a rule that separates evidence-driven updates from conversational pressure (S6 revise gate).

source: Samanta et al. (2026) BayesBench: Evaluating LLM Belief Trajectories Under Multi-Turn Evidence Accumulation
finding: Per-turn belief updates in coin-flip, recommender, social-judgment and triage tasks. Larger models track the hidden state better but over-react: they give more extreme probabilities than the Bayesian reference. Good latent inference does not carry over to downstream prediction.
numbers: 7 open-weight LLMs, 3B-70B; 4 environments; about 56 pages. Over-updating seen in the coin task and in triage labels pulled to extremes. Active engagement lowers calibration; the gap closes to noise only for Qwen-32B and LLaMA-70B.
limits: Meta/Columbia preprint, open-weight models only, no frontier models; exact per-model numbers were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Extending a belief each round tends to overshoot. Cap step size or keep rivals with scores instead of overwriting the mapping.

source: Ping et al. (2026) Why LLMs Give In: Conversational Factors and Reasoning Behind Medical Sycophancy
finding: A correct answer is abandoned more often when the false claim arrives as a later challenge than when it is in the first query. Fake sources raise sycophancy in single-turn but lower it in multi-turn. Putting the verified answer in the system prompt helps but does not remove it.
numbers: 48 conditions (4 roles x 3 evidence x 2 structure x 2 grounding), about 1.2M trials, 5 models. Multi-turn 6.99% vs single-turn 2.53% (2.8x). Single-turn: no source 1.99%, one 2.53%, several 3.08% (OR 1.46, 2.04). Multi-turn: 8.69%, 6.63%, 5.67% (OR 0.63, 0.49). GPT-OSS-120B under 1% in both. Epidemiology questions 16.59%.
limits: Medical QA, absolute rates are low (under 9%), five models. Variation is larger across questions than across models.
agent_relevance: A fixed grounded reference (a stored mapping the agent must consult) reduces flipping but does not remove it. Form of pushback matters.

source: Jenkins (2026) AGM-Bench: Do Large Language Models Revise Beliefs Rationally?
finding: Tests seven frontier LLMs on classical belief-revision postulates. They satisfy Success and Consistency but violate minimal change (Inclusion) and Preservation. Under repeated revision they keep retracted facts (inertia) and also drop unrelated beliefs (collateral damage). Reasoning-trained models are better on one step but degrade faster under iteration.
numbers: 2,400 synthetic scenarios, 6 AGM postulates plus Darwiche-Pearl postulates, 7 models. The page gives no per-model rates.
limits: Workshop abstract page only; no per-model numbers read; synthetic logic scenarios.
agent_relevance: Directly the update-versus-maintain trade-off for gap 4: after a conflicting fact, re-derive only the affected slots and re-check unrelated slots, not rewrite everything.

source: Liu et al. (2025) TRUTH DECAY: Quantifying Multi-Turn Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Accuracy falls across follow-up turns of user pushback. Initially wrong answers flip more than right ones. Subjective fields fall more than STEM.
numbers: Models: Claude Haiku, GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.1 8B. Initially wrong answers change up to 40% more than correct ones; 50% change by turn 4 vs about 10% stable for correct. Philosophy accuracy falls from about 70% to under 20%; STEM stabilises at 30-50%. Claude feedback sycophancy 76.74% to 30.23% by follow-up 7; OpenAI MMLU-Pro 49.30% to 26.76%. Abstract-level claim in conclusion: accuracy drops up to 47%.
limits: Three small or cheap models; student-led preprint; figures read from running text, not tables.
agent_relevance: Flipping compounds with rounds. A mapping held with low confidence is the one that flips; a score per slot lets the agent hold firm only where evidence is strong.

source: Guo et al. (2026) Stop Listening to Me! How Multi-turn Conversations Can Degrade LLM Reliability
finding: Stick-or-switch framework: splitting an answer space into sequential presentations lowers accuracy compared with presenting all options at once (a conversation tax). Models also switch from abstaining to correct and incorrect suggestions at similar rates (blind switching).
numbers: 17 LLMs, 3 clinical benchmarks. End-to-end accuracy below single-shot in 14/17 (MedQA), 14/17 (JAMA CC), 16/17 (MedMCQA). Tax up to 30% on average, 65% in some models. Llama 3 70B drops 17, 29, 17 pp. Blind switching up to 50%. Scale fixes some failures and worsens others.
limits: Clinical multiple choice; sequential incorrect hypotheses, not mapping facts.
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of sequential versus all-at-once presentation of competing hypotheses. Supports keeping rival mappings visible together rather than introducing them one by one.

source: Kim and Khashabi (2025) Challenging the Evaluator: LLM Sycophancy Under User Rebuttal
finding: Models endorse a counterargument more when it arrives as a user follow-up than when both answers are shown together for judging. Detailed reasoning in the rebuttal persuades even when wrong, and casual phrasing persuades more than a formal critique.
numbers: Persuasion rates (table text partly garbled): casual simple rebuttal 84.5%; follow-up rebuttal 56.1% average; are-you-sure 53.8%; neutral judge setting 43.6%.
limits: Table layout garbled, so cell-to-condition mapping is approximate; judgment tasks, not mapping.
agent_relevance: Present a new fact and the existing mapping side by side for a neutral comparison instead of as a correction in sequence.

source: Fanous et al. (2025) SycEval: Evaluating LLM Sycophancy
finding: Sycophancy in ChatGPT-4o, Claude Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro on math and medical advice. Most cases persist. Rebuttals placed before the answer cause more regressive sycophancy than in-context ones.
numbers: Sycophantic in 58.19% of cases (Gemini 62.47%, ChatGPT 56.71%). Progressive (to correct) 43.52%, regressive (to wrong) 14.66%. Preemptive 61.75% vs in-context 56.52% (Z=5.87, p<0.001). Regressive in computation: 8.13% vs 3.54%. Persistence 78.5% (95% CI 77.2-79.8).
agent_relevance: Not all flips are errors: 43.5% of sycophantic changes went toward the correct answer. The update gate must judge evidence, not block change.

source: Kandaswamy, Forbus, Gentner (2014) Modeling Learning via Progressive Alignment using Interim Generalizations
finding: Structure-mapping model reproduces Kotovsky and Gentner's progressive alignment effect: easy same-dimension comparisons first let the model re-represent and then succeed on hard cross-dimension triads. The control order (size-change only first) does not.
numbers: Two simulations of 16 triads each, qualitative match to 4-year-olds. Children 68% relational on the easiest triads vs model 100%. Experimental order gave far higher relational choice on cross-dimension triads than control. Assimilation threshold 0.95, interim generalization limit 5.
limits: Model only (no human data collected); model is too good on same-dimension triads and forms interim generalizations more readily than children; qualitative fit, no statistics; simple shapes. Original Kotovsky and Gentner 1996 numbers only second-hand. URL is the proceedings index, not the paper page.
agent_relevance: Close-to-far order has a symbolic computational precedent. No LLM test was found; the agent can try an easy-first example order.

source: Lovett, Gentner, Forbus, Sagi (2009) Using analogical mapping to simulate time-course phenomena in perceptual similarity
finding: Incremental encoding (attributes before relations) plus staged SME output reproduces three human time-course findings. A footnote says SME can update a mapping incrementally when new relations are encoded.
numbers: Human data cited: shield pairs 910 ms (low-similarity) vs 1270 ms (high-similarity) for a different response; Goldstone and Medin 1994 deadline results reproduced qualitatively. Three studies simulated.
limits: Human data are from other labs; qualitative fit only; footnote on incremental update is a remark, not a test.
agent_relevance: Early answers are feature-based, later answers relational: give a draft mapping early and verify relationally later, flagging drafts as provisional.

source: Khojasteh, Jiang, De Giorgis et al. (2026) Enhancing Structural Mapping with LLM-Derived Abstractions for Analogical Reasoning in Narratives (YARN)
finding: The related-work section says SME has recent extensions for greedy merging and incremental processing of new knowledge, and names FAME, an SME variant that combines LLM relation extraction with greedy beam-search mapping. YARN itself is still the only hybrid result found; no independent re-test.
numbers: No new numbers read beyond those already in b17 (Llama-3.1-8B 0.45 vs 0.28).
limits: Related-work text only for this line; gap 8 remains single-source.
agent_relevance: An SME variant with beam search is a cheap external mapper the agent could call; FAME is a second hybrid to look for.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs fall far short of Bayesian updating over rounds. Fine-tuning on a Bayesian assistant's predictions improves updating and transfers to new tasks.
numbers: Final-round accuracy figure labels around 66-80% in teaching conditions (figure text; condition mapping uncertain).
limits: Needs fine-tuning, so outside our no-training constraint; figure numbers not mapped to conditions.
agent_relevance: The gap can close but only by training; a scaffold has to compensate with explicit scores per slot.

source: Search record: replications of Keane, Ledgeway, Duff (1994) incremental-mapping order effect
finding: No replication found. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API returned HTTP 429 for every query in this session and the WebSearch budget was spent. The original (Keane et al. 1994, Cognitive Science) was not opened.
numbers: 0 replications found; 0 human order-effect N or statistics verified.
limits: Absence here is a tool limit, not evidence of absence in the literature.
agent_relevance: Treat the twofold order effect (K03) as one unreplicated human result.

source: Search record: Bridge Incremental Analogizer, Companion systems, SME 2016 incremental-session numbers
finding: No accuracy or speed numbers for incremental sessions found. Only passing references to incremental SME in d10 and d11 were read. Companion evaluation numbers already in the folder (Lovett and Forbus 2017, 56/60 on Raven's) are in claim K05.
limits: Forward-citation search could not be run.
agent_relevance: No evidence of a speed gain from extension over re-mapping outside the 1994 paper.

source: Search record: LLM tests of extend-versus-remap, joint candidate-inference checking, structured mapping tables
finding: Nothing found that tests extending a stored analogical mapping against re-mapping in an LLM, nor joint versus per-inference checking of candidate inferences. The nearest proxies are multi-turn degradation (Laban, in evidence a) and the sycophancy and belief-revision studies d01-d08.
limits: Few searches possible; a negative on the 2026 literature is weak.
agent_relevance: K14 (no direct test) stands; the agent's own A/B run is the only evidence we can get.

source: Goldstone and Medin (1994) and Sloutsky and Yarlas time-course data as reported by Lovett et al. (2009)
finding: Lovett et al. describe the deadline effects second-hand: at short deadlines judgments follow feature overlap; at longer deadlines relational alignment dominates; limited base-image encoding (150 ms vs 2100 ms) changes which target types win.
numbers: Encoding times 150 ms vs 2100 ms; deadline conditions up to 1.84 and 2.68 s.
agent_relevance: Supports staged mapping in the schema: shallow match first, relational check once budget allows.
